lesson.title: From Numbers to a Narrative: Writing Up a Statistical Study
lesson.summary: Teaches the structure and conventions of a complete statistical write-up, connecting calculations to context so a reader who never saw the raw data can trust and act on the conclusion.
lesson.body:
A calculation is not a conclusion until it is written into a sentence that a reader who never watched the analysis happen can understand and trust. Stating a decision in context, reject or fail to reject, or an interval of plausible values, is the seed of a full report, the skill you built while making conclusions throughout this course. A complete report does more work than that single sentence, though. It gives context, justifies the method chosen, and is honest about what the study cannot claim.

A solid statistical report generally has five parts. First, the purpose, framed as the actual parameter of interest and the question being asked. Second, a description of the data collection, who was studied, how, when, and how many. Third, the procedure used and why it fits, naming the test or interval and briefly noting that its conditions were checked. Fourth, the numerical results, the test statistic, the p-value or the confidence interval's endpoints. Fifth, a plain-language conclusion that answers the original question, along with any limitations and the scope to which the conclusion can be generalized.

Precise language matters as much as the structure. For a confidence interval, the template is close to fixed: we are C percent confident that the interval from this value to that value captures the true parameter, stated in context, not the sample statistic. For a hypothesis test, avoid saying the data proves anything, and never say there is a 5 percent chance the null hypothesis is true, a p-value is not that. Instead, write something like, because the p-value is less than or greater than alpha, we reject or fail to reject the null hypothesis, and there is or is not convincing evidence that the alternative claim, stated in context, is true.

Imagine a company testing a redesigned website by running a two-proportion z-test comparing the checkout completion rate of the old and new designs. A weak report would just say p equals 0.02, significant. A real report says something closer to this: among visitors sampled, the new design's completion rate was higher than the old design's. Because the p-value of 0.02 is less than alpha equals 0.05, there is convincing evidence that the new checkout page has a higher true completion rate than the old page, and a 95 percent confidence interval suggests the true improvement is somewhere between two and eleven percentage points. That last sentence, the interval, is what turns significant into a number a business can actually act on.

A trustworthy report keeps statistical significance and practical importance visibly separate, always reports an interval or effect size next to any point estimate, and states plainly who the conclusion does and does not apply to. That habit of never overselling what the data can support is what separates a report a decision-maker can rely on from one that simply recites numbers and hopes they sound convincing.
